summary: Defines the SNMPv2 management information base module for managing TCP implementations, so network tools can query connection tables and counters. It was replaced by RFC 4022.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a dashboard for TCP, the part of a computer that keeps conversations going. A manager can see how many are open.

questions: how to monitor tcp connections with snmp
subtitle: A dashboard for monitoring and managing TCP connections via SNMP.

tldr.problem: Network administrators needed a standard way to monitor and control TCP implementations on remote devices, but there was no consistent SNMP management information base (MIB) for TCP.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2012 defines a set of managed objects for TCP, including scalar values for retransmission timeout algorithms and limits, counters for connections and segments, and a table of active TCP connections with their state and endpoints.
tldr.outcome: This RFC provided the SNMPv2 version of the TCP MIB, replacing the earlier SNMPv1 MIB-II version. It was later replaced by RFC 4022 to support IPv6.

today: RFC 2012 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4022, which adds IPv6 support and other refinements. RFC 4022 is the current TCP MIB standard and is widely implemented in network devices, management platforms, and monitoring tools. The MIB remains essential for SNMP-based network management and is used by administrators and automated monitoring systems worldwide to track TCP behavior and diagnose connection issues.

sections.title: Introduction to the TCP MIB
sections.content: Network management requires a standard way to monitor and control network devices. The Management Information Base (MIB) is a virtual database of managed objects that a device exposes via SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol). A management station queries these objects to understand the device's state and can modify some objects to control behavior. This RFC defines the MIB module for managing TCP implementations, allowing administrators to monitor TCP behavior and settings on any device that supports SNMP. The managed objects in this module were originally defined using SNMPv1 as part of MIB-II. This RFC redefines them using SNMPv2 and the SMIv2 (Structure of Management Information version 2) notation, providing a cleaner and more extensible framework. Note that this MIB supports only IPv4 addresses (represented as 4-byte OCTET STRINGs); IPv6 support came later in RFC 4022.
sections.plainLanguage: A standard way to ask a computer 'How many TCP connections do you have right now?' or 'How many packets did you retransmit?' so managers can see what is happening with the network.

sections.title: TCP Scalar Objects and Counters
sections.content: The TCP MIB defines several scalar objects—single values that describe TCP's global behavior on a device. The tcpRtoAlgorithm object identifies which algorithm the device uses to compute retransmission timeouts (e.g., Van Jacobson's algorithm). tcpRtoMin and tcpRtoMax report the minimum and maximum retransmission timeout values in milliseconds, telling the manager how aggressively or conservatively the TCP implementation handles packet loss. tcpMaxConn reports the total number of TCP connections the entity can support (or -1 if dynamic). Beyond configuration, several counters track TCP activity: tcpActiveOpens counts transitions to SYN-SENT (when the local host initiates), tcpPassiveOpens counts transitions to SYN-RCVD (when the local host receives a connection request), tcpAttemptFails counts failed connection attempts, and tcpEstabResets counts connections abruptly reset from ESTABLISHED or CLOSE-WAIT. tcpCurrEstab is a gauge showing the current number of established or closing connections. tcpInSegs and tcpOutSegs are counters of all TCP segments received and sent, and tcpRetransSegs counts segments containing retransmitted octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Metrics like how many connections are open right now, how many are starting, how many failed, how many segments were sent and received, and how many had to be sent again.

sections.title: The TCP Connection Table
sections.content: Beyond global counters, the TCP MIB provides a table of all active TCP connections on the device: the tcpConnTable. Each row represents one connection and is indexed by four values: tcpConnLocalAddress (the local IPv4 address), tcpConnLocalPort (the local port), tcpConnRemAddress (the remote IPv4 address), and tcpConnRemPort (the remote port). For each connection, the table records tcpConnState, which can be one of twelve states: CLOSED, LISTEN, SYN-SENT, SYN-RCVD, ESTABLISHED, FIN-WAIT-1, FIN-WAIT-2, CLOSE-WAIT, LAST-ACK, CLOSING, TIME-WAIT, or deleteTCB. A management station can read the state of any connection and can set tcpConnState to deleteTCB to forcibly close the connection, causing the TCP layer to send a RST (reset) segment (though RST segments are not reliably delivered). Rows are transient: they exist only while the connection is open and disappear (shortly after) the connection closes. This allows a manager to monitor which hosts the device is communicating with and the status of each connection.
sections.plainLanguage: A list showing every open TCP connection: who you are talking to, which port on each end, and whether the connection is open, closing, waiting, or stuck.

sections.title: SNMP Management and Modern Updates
sections.content: RFC 2012 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1213 (the SNMPv1 MIB-II). It provides an SNMPv2 formulation using SMIv2, offering clearer semantics and better extensibility. The RFC notes that this MIB supports only IPv4 addresses and cannot manage IPv6 TCP connections; IPv6 support was added in RFC 4022, which is the current TCP MIB standard. Network management systems use these objects to create dashboards, alert on anomalies (e.g., high retransmit rates), perform capacity planning, and troubleshoot connection issues. The combination of scalar counters and the connection table gives administrators visibility into both the overall health of TCP on a device and the details of individual connections.
sections.plainLanguage: A standard way for network management tools to spy on TCP. Originally for IPv4 only, but later updated to handle IPv6 too. Managers use it to watch for problems and understand what is happening on the network.
